name: George Palmer Ransom

death.place: his 'old red mansion house', Plymouth, Luzerne Co., PA

updates.occupation: Farmer, mill owner; militia colonel; Revolutionary War veteran

events.title: Revolutionary service in his father's company
events.description: Orderly-sergeant in Capt. Samuel Ransom's Independent Company; 'gained some credit for his valor at Millstone, Boundbrook, Germantown and Brandywine'.

events.title: Captured by Indians
events.description: He had put on his best regimentals to go courting at old Benjamin Harvey's. Six Indians took the elder Harvey, his son Elisha, Lois (Louisa) Harvey, Lucy Bullford and Ransom; the women were released on Shawnee Mountain.

events.title: Imprisoned and escaped
events.description: Moved from Montreal to Prisoner's Island in Feb 1781; swam the St. Lawrence and, with two others, made his way through the forest to Vermont and then Connecticut. His account was taken down by Charles Miner as part of 'The Hazleton Travellers'.

events.title: Fined one cent for defending Washington's name
events.place: Luzerne County Court of Quarter Sessions, Wilkes-Barre
events.description: Pleaded guilty to knocking down a young man who had abused the name of General Washington. Judge Scott left the case to his associate judges (old soldiers Hollenback and Fell), who fined Ransom one cent and made the prosecutor pay costs.

events.title: Built a sawmill
events.description: Torn down in 1840 and replaced by his son Chester.

bioAdditions: Col. H. B. Wright lived next door to Colonel Ransom for twenty years. In his Historical Sketches of Plymouth (1873) he says Ransom was born at Canaan, Litchfield Co., Conn., in 1761. He served as orderly-sergeant in his father's company at Millstone, Bound Brook, Germantown and Brandywine. On 6 Dec 1780 he had gone 'a sparking' in his best regimentals to old Benjamin Harvey's house when six Indians burst in and carried off the household. After imprisonment on Prisoner's Island in the St. Lawrence he swam the river and escaped through the woods to Vermont. He lived and died in the 'old red mansion house' on the Plymouth flats, and the town pound stood on his land. Wright's book has his portrait 'taken at 85' (S1). Charles Miner noted in 1845 that he was 82 and lame, and that his grandson George Palmer Steele had just finished a term as sheriff of Luzerne (S3). A later county history tells how he was fined one cent for knocking down a man who had insulted Washington (S2). He built a sawmill in 1815, and his son Chester replaced it in 1840 (S3). One daughter married the schoolmaster Charles C. Curtis and inherited the Jackson Twp. farm (S1). Another, Livia, married Oliver Davenport (Bradsby).

conflicts.assessment: The sources disagree by a year or two. Wright, his neighbour, says 1761. Keep the site's 1762 as 'c.1761-62' unless a pension file decides it.

sources.supports: birth at Canaan, Conn., 1761; Revolutionary service as orderly-sergeant (Millstone, Bound Brook, Germantown, Brandywine); capture on 6 Dec 1780; imprisonment and escape; died in his red mansion house in Plymouth; daughter married Charles C. Curtis; portrait at 85. Wright was his next-door neighbor for 20 years.

researchLogEntry: Round 4: Wright 1873 gives b. Canaan, Conn., 1761, his war service, capture and escape, and the portrait at 85 (downloaded). Harvey & Smith give the one-cent-fine story; Bradsby gives the 1815 mill and grandson Sheriff George Palmer Steele.
